name: Walker Art Center
funding: Principal, US Bank, Best Buy, Cargill Foundation, 3M.
records_note: It posts annual reports for 2010-11 to 2024-25 with audited statements for 2024-25, names corporate supporters by tier undated, and lists its trustees.

name: Wellcome Collection
watch: Name to know: Wellcome Trust, whose fossil-fuel investments drew a 2015 divestment campaign; it sold BP and Shell shares in 2022.
why_flagged: Name to know: Wellcome Trust, whose fossil-fuel investments drew a 2015 divestment campaign; it sold BP and Shell shares in 2022.
records_note: No records of its own; its parent Wellcome Trust publishes annual reports and accounts 2019 to 2025 and its governors, and names no donors.

name: West Bund Museum
funding: Run and paid for by the state-owned West Bund Group. The Centre Pompidou partnership was renewed in 2023 for five years. Joint shows since 2019 drew over 2 million visitors.
watch: Local officials had fewer than five works removed from the 2019 opening show, The Shape of Time. Pompidou says it does not self-censor.
why_flagged: Run and paid for by the state-owned West Bund Group. The Centre Pompidou partnership was renewed in 2023 for five years. Joint shows since 2019 drew over 2 million visitors.
records_note: Its site could not be reached, so nothing was checked; the state-owned West Bund Group funds it under a five-year Pompidou partnership.

name: Wexner Center for the Arts
watch: Epstein-linked name; artist and grant withdrawals in 2026.
why_flagged: Ohio State arts centre founded by Les Wexner's 1987 gift of $1M and 100,000 L Brands shares. It takes $3.3M a year in grants and gifts; FY2025 revenue about $13M.
records_note: It posts annual reports for 2019-20 to 2024-25 that list donors by tier and its foundation board; Form 990 filings for the foundation are public.

name: Whanki Museum
funding: Private museum run by the Whanki Foundation, set up by the artist's widow Kim Hyang-an. No funder list or accounts found; the museum site fails its certificate check.
watch: In May 2026 residents and the Seoul Environment Alliance protested after herbicide was injected into a 200-year-old ginkgo beside the museum. It apologised.
why_flagged: Private museum run by the Whanki Foundation, set up by the artist's widow Kim Hyang-an. No funder list or accounts found; the museum site fails its certificate check.
records_note: Could not check: the museum site fails its security certificate and no register entry for the Whanki Foundation could be opened.

name: Whitechapel Gallery
funding: Arts Council England funds it. The 2021-22 report names Bloomberg Philanthropies, Max Mara, Swarovski Foundation and City Bridge Trust as major donors; Bloomberg and Phillips are corporate patrons.
watch: Historic East London public gallery founded in 1901.
why_flagged: Bloomberg Philanthropies is campaigned against elsewhere, not at Whitechapel. A 2006 Bellmer show lost works after self-censorship claims; no later case found.
records_note: No annual reports on its site; accounts are on the Charity Commission register, the Thank You page names donors undated, and trustees are listed.

name: Whitney Museum of American Art
funding: $105M annual operating budget. Admissions, board patron giving, Hyundai Motor, Tiffany & Co., Genesis philanthropic initiatives.
watch: Kanders resigned 2019 after protests; Crown family trustee targeted 2025.
why_flagged: Kanders resigned 2019 after protests; Crown family trustee targeted 2025.
records_note: It posts audited statements and Form 990s for 2014 to 2025, names its donors and lists 34 trustees as of October 2026.

name: Wiels Contemporary Art Centre
funding: Flemish, French-speaking, Brussels and VGC governments. Structural partners: Duvel Moortgat, Phillips, Aureus Ars & Scientia. Exhibition partners include Loterie Nationale and Gulbenkian France; GBL supports education.
watch: Independent non-profit operating on regional cultural subventions.
why_flagged: Flemish, French-speaking, Brussels and VGC governments. Structural partners: Duvel Moortgat, Phillips, Aureus Ars & Scientia. Exhibition partners include Loterie Nationale and Gulbenkian France; GBL supports education.
records_note: WIELS files accounts with the National Bank of Belgium, names its board and general assembly, and lists partners by name without a date.

name: Winzavod Centre for Contemporary Art
watch: Roman Trotsenko is on the EU list (June 2024) and the UK list (Feb 2025). His son Gleb is on the US list.
why_flagged: Private centre founded in 2007 by Roman and Sofia Trotsenko. Their Winzavod Foundation, led by Sofia, funds its programmes; they put their 2021 artist support at 15-20 million roubles.
records_note: Winzavod posts no annual report, accounts or board; its documents page holds policies and safety assessments, and partners show as logos with no date.

name: Württembergischer Kunstverein Stuttgart
funding: State of Baden-Württemberg Ministry of Science, Research and the Arts, City of Stuttgart; non-profit association.
watch: City withdrew a €15k symposium grant (2025-26) after antisemitism accusations; event went ahead on crowdfunding.
why_flagged: City withdrew a €15k symposium grant (2025-26) after antisemitism accusations; event went ahead on crowdfunding.
records_note: Württembergischer Kunstverein lists its administrative board and members but posts no annual report, accounts or funder list.

name: YARAT Contemporary Art Space
watch: Co-partnered a March 2026 exhibition with bp, SOCAR Midstream and PASHA Holding; funder roster itself not published.
records_note: No reports or accounts found; the partners page shows eight unnamed, undated logos, and the team page lists staff but no board.

name: Yeltsin Center
watch: Meduza (Mar 2026) reports average annual donations fell c. 14-fold in 2023–24 versus 2015–22. Its anti-war statement was deleted on police orders; events cancelled under pressure include Nina Khrushcheva's book launch (25 Nov 2024, after a Z-channel denunciation); KPRF bills to close it failed in the Duma.
why_flagged: Meduza (Mar 2026) reports average annual donations fell c. 14-fold in 2023–24 versus 2015–22. Its anti-war statement was deleted on police orders; events cancelled under pressure include Nina Khrushcheva's book launch (25 Nov 2024, after a Z-channel denunciation); KPRF bills to close it failed in the Duma.
records_note: The centre posts yearly accounting statements and names its trustees and board; it has no annual report and its partners page lists no sponsors.
